card.intuition: Parametric knowledge is what a model knows from training, stored in its parameters and frozen at training time. Reliability tracks how often a topic appeared in the data: dense topics reproduce accurately, rare topics blur into plausible guesses, and because reproducing and guessing are the same process to the model, it cannot tell which it is doing.
card.analogy: An engineer who ships a framework hundreds of times but has only a blurred impression of a vendor SDK encountered twice. For the familiar framework they recall precisely; for the rare SDK they extrapolate what it would look like and present the guess with the same confidence as real recall. The cure is the same either way: read the vendor's real docs into context.
card.time_complexity: O(C) per generated token over the full context window — parametric recall runs at inference speed, and supplying missing knowledge as context grows the per-request cost linearly with C.
card.space_complexity: Context/memory footprint: the parameters are fixed at training time, and the fix for a rare or stale topic must live in the window instead, where every loaded doc competes for the finite attention budget.
when_to_use: 'It writes flawless React but invents methods on our internal SDK' — React is dense in the training data, the SDK is not
Judging trust: how often a topic appeared in training predicts how accurately the model reproduces it, so rare topics deserve verification
Supplying knowledge the parameters lack: an internal SDK, a library released after the cutoff, or a decision made yesterday
Explaining why the model is fluent on common topics yet fabricates on uncommon ones
gotchas: No self-signal: the model cannot distinguish reproducing from guessing, so a fabricated answer sounds identical to a correct one
Parametric knowledge ages — parameters stop changing at the cutoff, and a library released after it does not exist in them
The parameters cannot be updated or read; the only fix for a rare or stale topic is to supply it as contextual knowledge

steps.label: Training squeezes facts
steps.annotation: Training adjusts parameters until the model predicts text well, and this squeezes billions of facts into a fixed parameter count.

steps.label: Common topics reproduce
steps.annotation: A topic with millions of examples is reproduced accurately because it is densely encoded in the parameters.

steps.label: Rare topics blur
steps.annotation: For a topic seen only a handful of times, the model guesses based on what similar topics look like.

steps.label: Guess sounds identical
steps.annotation: Reproducing and guessing are the same process to the model, so it cannot tell which one it is doing.

steps.label: Fix with context
steps.annotation: The parameters are frozen, so the missing knowledge has to be supplied as contextual knowledge in the window.

exercise.prompt: Decide whether parametric knowledge on a topic is reliable enough to trust, based on how often it appeared in training.
exercise.starter_code:
RELIABLE_THRESHOLD = 100_000

def reliably_recalled(examples):
    # Returns True when a topic appeared often enough in training data
    # for the model's parametric knowledge to reproduce it faithfully.
    return examples > ___________
hints: Frequent topics reproduce accurately; very rare ones turn into guesses.
Compare the example count against the reliability threshold constant.
exercise.test_code:
assert reliably_recalled(5_000_000) is True
assert reliably_recalled(12) is False
assert reliably_recalled(100_000) is False
print('PASS')
